skills.title: Name recognition
skills.goal: Turn toward you when their name is spoken in a quiet room.
skills.setup: Tiny rewards; a familiar quiet room.

steps.title: Make the name predict a reward
steps.teach: When your dog is relaxed near you, say their name once in a friendly voice, then immediately offer a tiny reward. No sit or eye contact is required. Pause a few seconds and repeat a handful of times; finish while they still enjoy it.
steps.advance: Your dog begins turning or expecting a reward after the name during several easy pairings.
steps.easier: Use a quieter room or a reward your dog readily enjoys. Do not repeat the name louder.

steps.title: Reward the head turn
steps.teach: With your dog comfortably looking slightly away, say their name once and pause briefly. As they turn toward you, reward beside your body. Reset by allowing them to look away again. You are teaching a head turn, not a long stare or a recall.
steps.advance: In this quiet room, turns toward you on 4 of 5 single-name opportunities in two short sessions.
steps.easier: Shorten the angle away from you; return to immediate name–reward pairings. Practice elsewhere is a separate module.

skills.title: Reward marker
skills.goal: Use a soft signal to identify a successful action.
skills.setup: Choose a signal that does not startle your dog.

steps.title: Pair the signal with food
steps.teach: Use your chosen soft marker once: say “yes,” use a physical clicker, or tap the app’s Mark & reward button. Immediately give a tiny treat. Pause before another pairing, and keep your reward hand still until after the signal. There is no action to ask for yet. Use the same signal consistently; if a click worries your dog, choose a gentle spoken word instead.
steps.advance: The signal produces relaxed reward anticipation in several pairings; no flinching or avoidance.
steps.easier: Soften the sound, change the signal, or deliver the reward directly without a marker.

skills.title: Hand target
skills.goal: Touch your open hand with the nose voluntarily.
skills.setup: Open palm held still beside, not over, the face.

steps.title: Capture a nose touch
steps.teach: Offer an empty palm a few inches from the side of your dog’s nose. Let them choose to sniff it. Say “yes” as the nose touches, then reward from the other hand. Remove the palm between attempts. Do not push your hand into their face.
steps.advance: Offers a gentle nose touch on 4 of 5 presentations without your palm moving toward them.
steps.easier: Start farther to the side, reward a small approach, or use an object target if hands worry them.

steps.title: Add the cue and a little movement
steps.teach: Say “touch,” then present your palm in the familiar position. Reward contact. Once that is easy, offer it just one small step to either side so the dog moves to reach it. Keep the reward hidden until after contact.
steps.advance: Touches on the cue/hand signal on 4 of 5 attempts in two short quiet sessions.
steps.easier: Return to a stationary nearby hand; avoid reaching across or steering the dog physically.

skills.title: Sit
skills.goal: Sit comfortably on a simple cue.
skills.setup: Non-slip surface; choose stand instead if sitting seems uncomfortable.

steps.title: Find a comfortable sit
steps.teach: Hold a tiny treat near the nose and slowly move it a little upward and back. When the bottom touches down, mark and feed. If the dog backs up, lower and shorten the motion. Never press the hips down. Alternatively, reward a naturally offered sit.
steps.advance: Can obtain a comfortable sit with a small hand motion on 4 of 5 attempts.
steps.easier: Capture an offered sit; use a non-slip surface. New stiffness or reluctance merits a vet conversation.

steps.title: Fade food in the guiding hand
steps.teach: Use the same motion with an empty hand. As the dog sits, mark and reward from your other hand or pouch. Then say “sit,” pause briefly, and give the familiar hand signal. Gradually make that signal smaller.
steps.advance: Responds to the chosen cue or small hand signal without a visible food lure on 4 of 5 attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Return briefly to an easy empty-hand signal; reward every success. Distance and distractions belong elsewhere.

skills.title: Lie down
skills.goal: Lie down comfortably on a cue.
skills.setup: Soft non-slip surface; no physical pushing.

steps.title: Guide or capture the down
steps.teach: From a comfortable stand or sit, guide a treat slowly toward the floor between the front paws, then slightly forward. Mark when elbows meet the surface and feed low. If the dog dislikes this route, wait for a natural comfortable lie-down and reward it.
steps.advance: Offers an unforced comfortable down several times using the chosen easy method.
steps.easier: Use a softer surface, a smaller motion, or capture natural downs. Skip postures that appear painful.

steps.title: Put down on a cue
steps.teach: Repeat the guiding motion with an empty hand and reward from your other hand. Once predictable, say “down” just before the hand signal. Over repetitions, pause after the word to let the dog respond before helping. Reset by inviting them to stand for a tossed reward.
steps.advance: Lies down on the chosen cue/signal, without a visible lure, on 4 of 5 attempts in two quiet sessions.
steps.easier: Make the hand signal clearer and use shorter sessions. Do not insist on a down near a frightening trigger.

skills.title: Stand
skills.goal: Stand up from a comfortable sit or down.
skills.setup: Non-slip floor; reward at standing nose height.

steps.title: Follow into standing
steps.teach: From a comfortable sit, move a treat slowly forward at nose height. Mark as all four feet support a stand, before the dog takes several steps. Feed in place. Repeat with an empty guiding hand, then put “stand” before that hand signal.
steps.advance: Stands on a small cue/signal without visible food on 4 of 5 attempts in two quiet sessions.
steps.easier: Shorten the lure distance and reward the first weight shift. Avoid repeated posture changes if stiff.

skills.title: Release from a position
skills.goal: Understand when a short requested position ends.
skills.setup: Start with a very easy one-second position. Use any comfortable sit, stand or down your dog already offers; a finished sit lesson is not required.

steps.title: Give the release meaning
steps.teach: After a very brief sit, stand, or down, say “free,” pause a beat, and toss a treat a small distance away. Let your dog move to it. On another repetition, reward the position first, then say “free” and invite movement.
steps.advance: Usually moves after the release word rather than requiring the tossed treat to start moving.
steps.easier: Use an easier position and a clear invitation to move; do not restrain the dog until released.

steps.title: Separate reward from release
steps.teach: Ask for a one-second position, feed in that position, then say “free” and invite movement. Sometimes give two in-position rewards before the release. Keep the interval easy so the dog can learn that a reward does not always end the position.
steps.advance: Can receive a reward in position, then move on “free” in 4 of 5 easy repetitions across two sessions.
steps.easier: Shorten the interval and make your release invitation clearer. Leaving due to discomfort is always allowed.

skills.title: Drop an item
skills.goal: Release an ordinary toy without confrontation.
skills.setup: A low-value dog-safe toy; no guarding history with this setup.

steps.title: Make releasing worthwhile
steps.teach: Let your dog hold an ordinary toy. Place a few tasty treats on the floor to the side; as the dog releases to eat, quietly mark the release. Let them have the toy again after the treats. Repeat a few easy exchanges. Never pry open the mouth or chase them.
steps.advance: Freely releases the low-value toy for the trade and remains loose around your approach.
steps.easier: Use a less-valued toy. If there is stiffness, growling, hovering over the item, or snapping, stop this setup and get individual help.

steps.title: Put the word before the trade
steps.teach: As your dog holds the easy toy, say “drop” once, then place the treats to the side. Reward the release and usually return the toy. Later pause a moment after “drop”; if they release before seeing food, mark and bring out the reward.
steps.advance: Releases the ordinary toy on one cue before food is shown on 4 of 5 attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Re-establish easy trades; do not test with stolen, dangerous, or treasured objects. Guarding is a separate problem.

skills.title: Leave an item alone
skills.goal: Turn away from an accessible-looking practice item before taking it.
skills.setup: Safe boring item behind a transparent container or otherwise out of reach.

steps.title: Reward turning away
steps.teach: Place a boring safe practice item where the dog can see but cannot grab it. Stay nearby with better rewards. Mark even a brief look away and feed away from the item. Reset with an easy approach. Do not use a valuable object that creates prolonged frustration.
steps.advance: Readily turns away from the protected item for a reward in 4 of 5 easy opportunities.
steps.easier: Make the item less interesting or start farther away; shorten the waiting time.

steps.title: Add the cue, then remove the barrier gradually
steps.teach: Say “leave” just before the familiar turn-away opportunity. Reward from you, away from the item. Once easy, use a safe item on the floor at more distance, with a leash/harness preventing accidental access without pulling. Reward the turn; reset before the dog approaches again.
steps.advance: Turns away on one cue from the selected safe floor item on 4 of 5 attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Replace the barrier or increase distance. Do not rehearse with toxic food or rely on this cue as your only safety measure.

skills.title: Short wait at an indoor doorway
skills.goal: Pause briefly before moving through a doorway together.
skills.setup: An interior door, open floor space, and no escape to outdoors.

steps.title: Reward a pause beside the doorway
steps.teach: At an open interior doorway, reward your dog for standing or sitting beside you for one second. Say “free” and move through together. Repeat until the pause is easy. Teach this beside a harmless doorway before involving an exterior door.
steps.advance: Offers a one-second pause with you in 4 of 5 easy repetitions.
steps.easier: Move farther from the doorway and shorten the pause. Avoid blocking the dog with your body.

steps.title: Add gentle door movement
steps.teach: Say “wait,” move the interior door only an inch, and reward the pause before releasing. Build opening width in small changes, keeping the pause short. If your dog moves, calmly reset farther back and use a smaller door movement; never swing it into them.
steps.advance: Can pause for a gentle full opening, then pass on release on 4 of 5 attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Use a smaller opening or no door movement. Continue using a leash/barrier at exterior doors regardless of training.

skills.title: Toilet routine
skills.goal: Use a predictable comfortable toilet location and tell you when needed.
skills.cue: Choose a toilet cue if useful
skills.setup: Regular access; investigate new accidents medically.

steps.title: Reward the right location
steps.teach: Offer a quiet toilet opportunity after waking, eating, play, and whenever your dog signals a need. Wait without pressuring them. As they finish in the chosen area, quietly reward there, then allow a little sniff time. Clean accidents without punishment.
steps.advance: A routine reliably creates successful opportunities; record the timing of any accidents to adjust access.
steps.easier: Offer more frequent easy access. Sudden accidents, straining, or increased drinking warrant a vet check.

steps.title: Add a cue and an easy request
steps.teach: Say your chosen toilet cue softly as elimination begins, then reward completion. If you want a request signal, reinforce a simple approach to the door by promptly offering a toilet trip; do not demand a long wait or a trick before access.
steps.advance: Uses the usual toilet area reliably with the planned routine; any request signal leads to a prompt opportunity.
steps.easier: Keep the schedule even if a request signal is not learned. Never delay access to test reliability.

skills.title: Come when called, first at home
skills.goal: Return over a short quiet distance to a rewarding handler.
skills.setup: Secure room; hidden rewards; never punish arrival.

steps.title: Build a short return
steps.teach: With your dog near you, say your recall word, take a welcoming step backward, and reward as they reach you. Reset by tossing a treat a little away, then call when they are easily able to return. Keep the cue different from their name.
steps.advance: Returns over one or two steps in 4 of 5 quiet repetitions.
steps.easier: Start closer and with less competing activity. Do not chase the dog or repeat a cue unlikely to succeed.

steps.title: Make arrival comfortable and worthwhile
steps.teach: Gradually call over a few more steps in the same quiet space. Deliver several small rewards at your side, then release the dog back to an enjoyable activity. Separately pair a brief gentle harness touch with food so arrival need not lead to grabbing or ending all fun.
steps.advance: Returns promptly over the chosen short indoor distance on 4 of 5 attempts across two sessions.
steps.easier: Shorten distance or reward more generously. If harness touching worries the dog, train that separately rather than adding it to recalls.

skills.title: Nose target an object
skills.goal: Touch a broad, safe target with the nose.
skills.setup: A large smooth target pad on a stable handle; no sharp ends or detachable small parts.

steps.title: Discover the target
steps.teach: Hold the target still a little to the side of the dog’s nose. Let them choose to investigate. Mark a gentle nose contact and reward from your other hand. Remove the target after each attempt; do not poke it toward the face.
steps.advance: Voluntarily touches the still pad in 4 of 5 easy presentations.
steps.easier: Use a larger target, increase space, or reward a glance or small approach first.

steps.title: Add a cue and vary placement
steps.teach: Say “target,” then present the familiar pad. Reward nose contact. Once this is easy, change the pad’s position by a few inches, staying at a comfortable head height. Return to the easiest placement between small changes.
steps.advance: Touches the pad on cue in two short sessions, with 4 of 5 comfortable responses.
steps.easier: Keep the pad stationary and closer. Stop if the dog starts mouthing or avoiding it.

skills.title: Go to a mat
skills.goal: Move onto a mat on cue; relaxation is taught separately.
skills.setup: Comfortable non-slip mat, away from triggers.

steps.title: Make the mat worth approaching
steps.teach: Lay out the mat and let your dog investigate. Mark a step toward or onto it and place the reward on the mat. Reset by tossing a reward off, then wait for another voluntary approach. Gradually reward paws on the mat rather than merely looking at it.
steps.advance: Voluntarily returns with all four paws on the mat on 4 of 5 resets.
steps.easier: Use a larger flatter mat and reward a smaller approach. Check that texture or slipping is not worrying them.

steps.title: Add the mat cue
steps.teach: Say “mat” just before your dog starts toward it, then reward on the mat. Later cue from one step away without tossing food onto it first. Accept comfortable standing, sitting, or lying here; the goal is reaching the target, not staying or relaxing yet.
steps.advance: Goes onto the mat on the cue from one step away, without visible food, in 4 of 5 attempts across two sessions.
steps.easier: Move closer or help with a small hand gesture, then fade it.

skills.title: Relax voluntarily on the mat
skills.goal: Rest with soft body language, rather than simply hold a down.
skills.setup: Work after ordinary needs are met; dog can leave.

steps.title: Capture comfortable resting
steps.teach: Place the familiar mat near you during a quiet activity. When your dog chooses a comfortable lie-down, gently place a reward between the paws. Watch for soft eyes, an easy hip shift, or a head resting. Reward quietly so you do not turn this into excited repetition.
steps.advance: Chooses to rest with visibly soft posture on several occasions; can leave and return freely.
steps.easier: Use a quieter place or a preferred bed. Reward subtle softening; do not keep asking for down.

steps.title: Stretch a restful interval
steps.teach: While your dog is already resting comfortably, vary the pause between quiet rewards: briefly longer, then easier again. Stop feeding if it repeatedly makes them pop up; try a less exciting reward or simply quiet companionship. End before rest becomes an effort.
steps.advance: Remains comfortably resting for about 30 seconds across two easy sessions, without rigid staring for food.
steps.easier: Shorten the interval and reduce nearby activity. A dog holding still while tense has not met this criterion.

steps.title: Pair an optional settle word
steps.teach: Softly say “settle” as your dog begins a familiar relaxed rest, then let the calm experience continue. After several pairings, try saying it just before sitting down nearby. Do not use it to require immobility when the dog needs space.
steps.advance: The word predicts a familiar easy rest; the dog can soften and stay comfortable in this original quiet setting.
steps.easier: Keep capturing natural rest without adding a cue. Distracting locations belong in Practice elsewhere.

skills.title: Choose a safe resting area
skills.goal: Voluntarily use a refuge without expecting interruption.
skills.setup: Quiet room or open crate only if already comfortable; water and a bed.

steps.title: Build a pleasant refuge
steps.teach: Set up a quiet resting area away from windows or the entryway. Let your dog explore; place a little normal food there and allow them to leave. Spend calm time nearby. Do not close a crate or room door if confinement is unfamiliar or distressing.
steps.advance: Enters and rests or explores freely in several quiet visits; there is no hesitation about returning.
steps.easier: Use an open room or bed instead of a crate. Move it farther from sounds or household traffic.

steps.title: Practice brief separation from activity
steps.teach: While someone stays with the dog or remains comfortably visible, reduce the outside activity with a gate, partly closed door, or curtains only to a degree they already tolerate. Reward comfortable participation. Gradually try your normal visitor-management arrangement without an actual visitor.
steps.advance: Comfortable in the chosen arrangement during several brief rehearsals across two sessions; no confinement distress.
steps.easier: Leave the door open or keep trusted company with them. A closed-door refuge is unsuitable if it causes panic.

skills.title: Very brief comfortable alone time
skills.goal: Practice small absences without distress; not a full panic-treatment program.
skills.setup: Camera; a familiar safe area; skip to individual help if absences already cause panic.

steps.title: Find an easy starting movement
steps.teach: With the camera positioned, begin while your dog is comfortably occupied or resting. Stand up or take one step away, then return before they worry. Observe posture, movement, and breathing, rather than requiring a stay. Repeat only a few easy movements with breaks.
steps.advance: Can make that small movement repeatedly without vigilance, following in distress, or other signs of worry.
steps.easier: Make the movement smaller or remain seated. For known separation panic, arrange professional support instead of testing their limit.

steps.title: Try a moment out of view
steps.teach: Once moving within the room is easy, briefly lean beyond an interior doorway and return immediately. Watch the camera. Build tiny intervals below the onset of worry and mix easier repetitions into practice. Do not increase on every trial.
steps.advance: Several comfortable tiny absences in two sessions, with ordinary behavior throughout and after your return.
steps.easier: Reduce the absence to less than a second or return to in-view movements. Do not wait for crying to stop before returning.

steps.title: Separate departure cues from duration
steps.teach: If a tiny absence is comfortable, practice one departure action, such as touching keys, without leaving. On another occasion, repeat the easy absence without extra cues. Only combine them after both are comfortable. Long actual departures need their own supported plan.
steps.advance: The selected departure action and tiny absence are both comfortable; a longer plan is set to the individual dog.
steps.easier: Drop the departure action or shorten the absence. Persistent pacing, escape attempts, or distress means pause and seek individualized care.

skills.title: Rest the head on a cushion
skills.goal: Place the chin briefly on a low comfortable cushion.
skills.setup: A low stable soft cushion; no lifting or positioning the head. Chin placement is not proof of relaxation.

steps.title: Discover the cushion target
steps.teach: Place the cushion at a comfortable natural chin height with the dog able to leave. Mark any voluntary chin contact and reward gently beside it. A known chin-rest invitation can help, but never lift or press the head into position.
steps.advance: Voluntarily lowers the chin onto the cushion several times without tension or restraint.
steps.easier: Use a flatter cushion, reward a small head dip, or return to a familiar hand chin rest.

steps.title: Name a brief rest
steps.teach: Say “rest” before the familiar voluntary chin placement. Reward a moment of soft contact, then invite a break. Add only a second when comfortable. Keep observing the whole dog: a chin on a cushion can be an action without emotional calm.
steps.advance: Places and briefly rests the chin on the cushion on cue while freely lifting away.
steps.easier: Shorten contact or skip the cue and reward spontaneous comfortable resting instead.

skills.title: Voluntary check-in
skills.goal: Choose to glance toward you during an easy walk.
skills.setup: Familiar secure space; rewards at your side.

steps.title: Catch offered attention
steps.teach: Stand or stroll in a quiet enclosed area. Whenever your dog voluntarily glances toward you, mark and reward beside you. Let them return to sniffing. Avoid constantly calling their name; the choice to check in is what earns the reward.
steps.advance: Offers several check-ins without being called, with loose comfortable movement.
steps.easier: Start indoors, stand still, or shorten the exercise. Sniffing does not need to stop all session.

steps.title: Reward while moving
steps.teach: Walk a few relaxed steps, then reward a voluntary glance while continuing slowly or pausing. Release back to sniffing often. Build short stretches with the leash loose; this is not a formal heel or a requirement to stare at you.
steps.advance: Offers check-ins during several short quiet walks, without repeated cueing or tension.
steps.easier: Reduce movement and nearby distractions. Trigger work is taught on its own tab.

skills.title: Loose-leash walking
skills.goal: Move together with slack in the leash.
skills.setup: Comfortable fitted harness; ordinary leash; quiet practice route.

steps.title: Reward the starting zone
steps.teach: In a quiet area, reward your dog for standing near either chosen side with slack in the leash. Place the reward at your leg rather than out in front. Reset by moving one step and reward the dog for coming back into that comfortable area.
steps.advance: Readily finds the side position with a loose leash in several short repetitions.
steps.easier: Practice indoors first; check equipment comfort and use a wider space.

steps.title: Add a few steps
steps.teach: Take one or two steps and reward before the leash tightens. Gradually mix two, three, and easier one-step stretches. If your relaxed dog pulls toward an ordinary interesting spot, pause, invite them back gently, and restart more easily. Never jerk the leash.
steps.advance: Can complete five to ten easy steps with slack on most attempts across two sessions.
steps.easier: Increase reward frequency or shorten the route. If fear is driving pulling, move to safety instead of standing still.

steps.title: Use permission to sniff as a reward
steps.teach: Walk a few loose steps toward a safe sniffing area, then say a release cue and let your dog explore. Alternate walking and sniffing so staying near you does not mean losing all choices. Keep sessions short enough to prevent frustration.
steps.advance: Repeatedly moves between loose walking and allowed sniffing in this quiet setting.
steps.easier: Choose less exciting sniff spots and shorten the walking portion. New locations belong in Practice elsewhere.

skills.title: Happy turn-away
skills.goal: Turn and travel away with you before a difficult encounter.
skills.setup: Teach first with no trigger; enough space for a wide turn.

steps.title: Teach the turn without a trigger
steps.teach: In a quiet room or yard, say “this way” cheerfully, turn your shoulders, and take two steps away. Reward your dog beside you as they follow. If needed, guide the first few repetitions with a treat, then hide it until after the turn.
steps.advance: Follows the cue into a comfortable turn without a visible lure on 4 of 5 easy repetitions.
steps.easier: Use a smaller change of direction, slower steps, or an easy hand target.

steps.title: Add the leash and an exit destination
steps.teach: In a quiet outdoor space, cue the turn with the leash slack. Move several steps to a chosen safe destination and reward there. Practice both directions, keeping your body and leash clear of the dog’s feet. Rehearse exits before you need them.
steps.advance: Can turn and travel several steps in either direction on 4 of 5 quiet rehearsals in two sessions.
steps.easier: Return to the yard and reward after fewer steps. A surprise encounter may still require immediate management rather than a cue.

steps.title: Rehearse a gentle planned interruption
steps.teach: During an easy sniff on a quiet route, cue the practiced turn and reward generous movement away. Choose moments the dog can easily leave. Keep most rehearsals free of triggers so the cue continues to predict something pleasant.
steps.advance: Responds during easy ordinary sniffing in 4 of 5 trials across two sessions, without leash pressure.
steps.easier: Choose a less interesting sniff and shorten the travel. Do not test beside a dog that already frightens them.

skills.title: Find food on the ground
skills.goal: Search for a few safe scattered treats on cue.
skills.setup: Clean surface; one dog only; no traffic or food competition.

steps.title: Pair the cue with a visible scatter
steps.teach: Say “find it,” then scatter a few tiny treats over a small clean area where your dog can see them land. Let them sniff and finish without pressure. Repeat in a calm familiar place. This is an activity, not a requirement to stop feeling afraid.
steps.advance: Begins searching after the cue in several easy scatters and stays comfortable.
steps.easier: Use a smaller clean area or place food visibly. Skip food games where guarding or competition is present.

steps.title: Move the search to an easy outdoor spot
steps.teach: Use the cue on clean ground in a quiet yard, then a quiet familiar outdoor spot. Keep pieces easy to find and away from paths. Continue practicing without triggers; use a barrier and distance before considering it during a difficult encounter.
steps.advance: Can search comfortably on the selected outdoor surface and rejoin you after finishing.
steps.easier: Return to a familiar surface or hand-deliver rewards instead. Do not scatter if an approaching dog could reach the food.

skills.title: Move behind you or to the far side
skills.goal: Take a comfortable position on the side away from passing activity.
skills.setup: A quiet room; an already comfortable hand target.

steps.title: Guide the side change
steps.teach: Stand still and present your hand target beside your far leg. Let your dog walk around you to touch it; mark and feed there. Keep the route wide and unobstructed. Repeat both ways without crossing or tightening a leash.
steps.advance: Can move to the other side with a small target presentation on most quiet attempts.
steps.easier: Use a wider arc and fewer steps. Do not move your hand over or into the dog.

steps.title: Add a cue and short movement
steps.teach: Say “other side,” then offer the known target beside the far leg. Fade the target to a small gesture. After arrival, take one step together and reward. This position is an optional management aid, not protection against an approaching loose dog.
steps.advance: Moves to the requested side and follows one or two steps on 4 of 5 quiet attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Return to a stationary target. Increase distance from real activity rather than trying to hold this position too close.

skills.title: Seeing a dog predicts good things
skills.goal: Feel comfortable observing another dog from an individually suitable distance.
skills.setup: Open space, clear exit, secure comfortable equipment; cooperative helper and calm adult dog if arranging practice.

steps.title: Find a comfortable viewing setup
steps.teach: Choose a wide quiet area where you can retreat without passing the other dog. Begin farther away than you think necessary. Allow one brief distant sighting, then leave the view. Record distance and body language without approaching to find the breaking point. Both dogs and handlers need to be comfortable.
steps.advance: Can notice the helper dog with loose movement and ordinary interest, then return to baseline when the view ends.
steps.easier: Start farther away or use a partial visual barrier. If no comfortable setup is available, use management and individual professional help.

steps.title: Pair the sight with food
steps.teach: At the easy distance, let your dog notice the other dog; promptly feed several tiny desired treats. When the helper goes out of view, let the feeding pause. No sit, silence, or eye contact is required. Allow a break and repeat only after the dog has returned to baseline.
steps.advance: Across two sessions, several brief sightings stay comfortable and the dog begins relaxed food anticipation on seeing the helper.
steps.easier: Increase distance or shorten the glimpse. If a bark or startle occurs, help them leave and simplify; do not withhold food as punishment.

steps.title: Vary one easy feature
steps.teach: Keep the safe distance and have the helper take one slow step sideways, then stop. Pair the sight/movement with food as before. Mix still, easier sightings between moving ones. On a later day you may change distance slightly instead, while keeping movement easy.
steps.advance: Several comfortable observations in two sessions at this one new version, with recovery no slower than the easy baseline.
steps.easier: Remove the movement or return to the previous distance. Reduced distance is optional; comfortable coexistence is the goal.

skills.title: Choose to look away from another dog
skills.goal: Voluntarily disengage without being repeatedly called.
skills.setup: Use the already comfortable DOG setup; do not wait through fixation.

steps.title: Reward a brief offered turn-away
steps.teach: After easy sight–food pairings, allow a tiny natural pause if your dog remains loose. If they turn their head away, sniff normally, or glance toward you, mark that choice and reward. If attention starts to become sticky, move farther away and continue simple pairing rather than waiting them out.
steps.advance: Offers several easy turn-aways while still able to observe and move comfortably.
steps.easier: Return to sight–food pairings at greater distance. Do not demand eye contact or interrupt every glance at the dog.

steps.title: Practice a choice and retreat
steps.teach: Reward an offered turn-away, then calmly walk a few steps farther from the helper together. Let the dog sniff and recover. Re-enter the easy view only if they remain willing. Alternate simple pairings with these choice-and-retreat repetitions.
steps.advance: Voluntarily disengages on most easy sightings across two sessions, with loose movement away and ordinary recovery.
steps.easier: Make the sighting shorter and retreat sooner. A turn caused by leash pressure does not count as the chosen behavior.

skills.title: Walk parallel at a comfortable distance
skills.goal: Move in the same direction as a helper dog without needing contact.
skills.setup: Two capable handlers, wide quiet space, no convergence; individualized help for aggression or redirection.

steps.title: Add parallel movement
steps.teach: After a comfortable stationary sighting, have both handlers walk in the same direction at the established wide separation. Keep the dogs from converging. Walk only a few steps, reward comfortable observation or check-ins, then curve farther apart for a break.
steps.advance: Both dogs remain comfortable through several short parallel stretches and recover normally after breaks.
steps.easier: Increase separation and shorten the stretch, or return to stationary sightings. Do not walk directly toward each other.

steps.title: Extend the easy stretch
steps.teach: Repeat short parallel stretches at the successful separation. Gradually lengthen only the walking portion, keeping direction and speed predictable. Give regular sniff breaks apart. Decrease separation on a separate day only if that is useful and both dogs remain comfortable.
steps.advance: Completes practical short parallel stretches in two sessions without tension building or recovery slowing.
steps.easier: Use shorter stretches or a wider route. This exercise does not require or imply readiness for a greeting.

skills.title: Make a wide planned pass
skills.goal: Pass a controlled helper at a comfortable practical distance.
skills.setup: An exit route and two handlers; no narrow paths or surprise dogs.

steps.title: Rehearse a staged pass
steps.teach: Position the helper well away from your walking line. Start with a stationary dog, then walk a short arc across the distant view. Reward your dog after noticing the helper and for comfortable movement. Complete the pass by moving into clear space, not by stopping close to the helper.
steps.advance: Several brief staged passes stay comfortable across two sessions, with full recovery and no pressure to approach.
steps.easier: Widen the arc, hide the helper partly, or return to parallel walking. Stop if either dog becomes tense.

steps.title: Try a gentle opposite-direction pass
steps.teach: Have the helper move slowly on a separate distant line while you use the same wide arc. Keep the total duration short and exits clear. Reward as needed; use the practiced turn to leave early if attention hardens. Repeat with the same helper before changing identities or locations.
steps.advance: Comfortable wide passes with this helper in this setting across two sessions; practical distance is recorded.
steps.easier: Restore a stationary helper or greater separation. Unexpected real-world encounters remain management situations.

skills.title: Feel safer with an unfamiliar adult
skills.goal: Observe a person without pressure to greet.
skills.setup: One cooperative adult, safe distance, open retreat, no children as training helpers.

steps.title: Start with an uninteresting person
steps.teach: Arrange for a cooperative adult to stand or sit sideways at a generous distance and ignore the dog. Let your dog notice for a brief moment, then give desired food yourself and allow retreat. The person does not approach, reach, stare, or offer food to lure the dog closer.
steps.advance: Several brief views are comfortable, with voluntary movement and ordinary recovery between them.
steps.easier: Increase distance, shorten the view, or add a visual barrier. Do not keep the dog near a person just because they eat.

steps.title: Make one small movement predictable
steps.teach: At the comfortable setup, have the adult shift one hand slightly, then stop. Feed promptly after the movement; pause when it ends. Repeat only after baseline returns. Other sessions can separately introduce a quiet word, a hat, or standing up partway—one change at a time.
steps.advance: The selected tiny movement is comfortable across several observations in two sessions.
steps.easier: Remove that movement or make it smaller and farther away. A dog can remain separate for visits.

steps.title: Practice with a second adult separately
steps.teach: Use the original easy distance and stationary setup with a different cooperative adult. Rebuild the positive pairing instead of assuming the first person’s progress transfers. Keep retreat available. Moving closer or accepting touch is optional and should not be the default next test.
steps.advance: Comfortable observations of more than one adult in separate easy sessions; individual differences are recorded.
steps.easier: Treat the new person as a fresh starting point. For threatening behavior, keep separation and get an individualized plan.

skills.title: Feel comfortable hearing a knock
skills.goal: Hear controlled knocking without escalating anxiety.
skills.setup: No actual arrivals; prevent surprise knocking while practicing.

steps.title: Pair a very soft tap
steps.teach: Sit with your dog well away from the entrance. Make one barely audible fingertip tap on a surface that does not alarm them, then promptly provide a tiny desired reward. Pause long enough for ordinary behavior to return. Do only a few comfortable repetitions; nobody comes in.
steps.advance: Several gentle taps predict relaxed interest or food anticipation across two short sessions.
steps.easier: Use a softer surface, a helper farther away, or a quieter recording. Stop if the tap already worries the dog.

steps.title: Transfer to the actual door
steps.teach: Have a helper make one very soft tap at the real door while you stay with the dog at the successful distance. Feed promptly after the sound, without waiting for a sit or quiet. Keep the door closed. Start easier than you think necessary because the location changes the meaning.
steps.advance: Comfortable brief actual-door taps in two sessions, with full return to baseline between them.
steps.easier: Make the tap softer or move the dog farther into the home. Use management for deliveries and ordinary guests.

steps.title: Change one part of the knock
steps.teach: At the successful setup, add a second soft tap; on a later occasion try a slightly stronger single tap instead. Keep repetitions sparse and stop while the dog is comfortable. Your objective is a practical gentle knock response, not tolerating maximum-volume banging.
steps.advance: The chosen realistic knock pattern is comfortable across two sessions; no escalating vigilance or prolonged recovery.
steps.easier: Return to a single faint tap. Knocking-to-mat and actual visitors are separate skills.

skills.title: Feel comfortable hearing the doorbell
skills.goal: Build a positive response to the actual bell sound.
skills.setup: Controllable recording first; someone can operate the real bell on request.

steps.title: Start with a faint recording
steps.teach: Record your bell or choose a similar sound. Play a very brief faint version once, then promptly feed a desired treat. Wait for baseline before repeating. If the dog does not notice the sound, avoid raising it rapidly; make one tiny change at a time.
steps.advance: Several noticeable faint sounds remain comfortable and predict relaxed reward anticipation.
steps.easier: Move the speaker farther away or reduce volume. A recording may not sound like the actual bell to the dog.

steps.title: Transfer carefully to the actual bell
steps.teach: Use a helper to produce the briefest controllable real bell sound while your dog is far from the entrance. Pair the sound promptly with food and keep the door shut. If the bell cannot be made easy enough, keep it disabled for management and use professional help for the gradient.
steps.advance: The selected real-bell setup is comfortable in several observations across two sessions.
steps.easier: Return to the recording or create more distance/insulation. A real visitor is not included in this stage.

skills.title: Knock means go to the mat
skills.goal: Link a comfortable knock to a known mat action.
skills.setup: Dog is already comfortable with the selected knock; no visitors yet.

steps.title: Link the two familiar events
steps.teach: Use the easy knock once, pause briefly, then say “mat.” Reward on the mat as your dog arrives. Release after a moment. Keep the knock intensity and mat distance easy. If the knock changes the dog’s emotional state, return to KNOCK rather than repeating the chain.
steps.advance: Can hear the easy knock, follow “mat,” and receive rewards there comfortably on 4 of 5 repetitions in two sessions.
steps.easier: Reduce the knock or put the mat closer. Practice the two components separately.

steps.title: Let the knock become the cue
steps.teach: Repeat knock, short pause, mat cue. Occasionally wait an extra beat after the knock: if your dog starts toward the mat, quietly reward arrival without adding the word. If not, help with the familiar word. Gradually use the word less, without increasing sound difficulty.
steps.advance: Goes to the mat after the selected knock without the extra word on 4 of 5 comfortable trials across two sessions.
steps.easier: Use the word again and shorten the pause. Do not wait while the dog scans or becomes worried.

steps.title: Add your own doorway movement
steps.teach: After an easy knock and mat arrival, take one step toward the closed entry door, return, and reward on the mat. Build to touching the handle, then a tiny opening with a separate secure barrier preventing access. No person enters yet.
steps.advance: Remains comfortable during your planned handle/opening rehearsal across two sessions; the physical barrier remains in place.
steps.easier: Reduce your movement or keep the door shut. The mat is not a substitute for a secure barrier.

skills.title: Comfortable separated visitor routine
skills.goal: Coexist with a visitor through a planned separated setup.
skills.setup: Cooperative adult; trusted company if needed; secure barrier; no bite-risk exposure without professional support.

steps.title: Rehearse without a visitor
steps.teach: Practice moving your dog into their comfortable refuge before you touch the entry door. Give a suitable activity if enjoyed; someone may stay with them. Rehearse opening and closing the entryway while the dog stays safely separated and comfortable.
steps.advance: The whole no-visitor arrangement is comfortable on several rehearsals in two sessions.
steps.easier: Keep more trusted company, more distance, or an open interior view. Do not use confinement that causes panic.

steps.title: Bring in one quiet adult while separated
steps.teach: Arrange a no-knock arrival. Settle your dog in the refuge first, then admit the cooperative adult, who sits quietly away from it. Stay with or monitor the dog. Pair any noticed mild arrival sounds with desired rewards; end the visit before distress develops.
steps.advance: Dog remains comfortable through several short quiet separated visits; duration and any sounds are recorded.
steps.easier: Shorten the visit, increase sound insulation or distance, or keep the adult outside. Greeting is unnecessary.

steps.title: Offer an optional distant view
steps.teach: Only if safe and your dog is comfortable with STRANGER practice, offer a brief distant view of the seated adult through a secure barrier. You supply food; the adult ignores the dog. End the view while comfortable and return to the refuge. Staying fully separated is also a successful long-term option.
steps.advance: Several optional views are comfortable with easy retreat and normal recovery across two visits.
steps.easier: Skip the view or shorten it. A dog that approaches for food has not necessarily invited touch.

steps.title: Add one visitor action
steps.teach: At the successful separated/viewing arrangement, ask the adult to say one quiet word or shift slightly, then stop. Pair the event with food. On separate visits, try standing partway or leaving. Return to the easier arrangement with each new person.
steps.advance: Comfortable observations of the selected action over two visits; no pressure to approach or remove the barrier.
steps.easier: Use a smaller action, greater separation, or no view. Escalation or bite concerns require an individual plan.

skills.title: Four paws greeting with familiar people
skills.goal: Greet a person the dog already wants to meet without jumping.
skills.setup: Only a comfortable familiar adult; this is not stranger-fear treatment.

steps.title: Reward four paws before approach
steps.teach: With a familiar adult at an easy distance, reward your dog for standing with all four paws down. Have the adult take one slow step closer; reward before jumping begins. The adult pauses or steps back if needed so you can reset at an easier distance.
steps.advance: Keeps four paws on the floor for several tiny familiar-person approaches without frustration or fear.
steps.easier: Shorten the approach and reward lower. If jumping reflects distress, work on feelings and space instead.

steps.title: Offer a brief optional hello
steps.teach: When the approach is easy, let your dog choose a brief greeting. The adult may gently stroke a shoulder only if the dog seeks it, then pause. Reward four paws and allow the dog to leave. Make the next repetition shorter if excitement builds.
steps.advance: Several comfortable short greetings in two sessions, with four paws down and an easy exit.
steps.easier: Use no touching and a briefer approach. Nobody leans over, restrains, or demands a greeting.

skills.title: Controlled sound practice
skills.goal: Build a positive association with one adjustable sound.
skills.setup: One chosen sound; controllable speaker; quiet home; stop playback immediately if needed.

steps.title: Find a faint noticeable version
steps.teach: Choose just one sound and record the starting volume/speaker position. Play a split-second faint version from a distance. If it is noticed comfortably, promptly offer desired food. End playback and allow a break. Do not loop a track while waiting for the dog to stop reacting.
steps.advance: Several noticeable faint presentations stay comfortable across two sessions.
steps.easier: Reduce volume, shorten the clip, or move the speaker farther away. No reaction to a recording may mean it is not meaningful to this dog.

steps.title: Change one sound feature
steps.teach: Repeat the successful sound–food pairing. Make only one small change: slightly longer OR slightly louder, while all else stays easy. Include easier trials. Stop the sound and simplify if posture tightens, scanning increases, or recovery takes longer.
steps.advance: Comfortable observations at the selected new setting in two sessions, with ordinary recovery between them.
steps.easier: Return to the original setting or choose a more controllable sound; do not increase until the dog reacts.

steps.title: Try a modest realistic variation
steps.teach: Keep the session easy while changing just the sound source or location slightly, such as the same recording played farther from another doorway. Rebuild from the quiet version. Real outdoor events and storms require their own management and cannot be certified safe by recording progress.
steps.advance: The specific realistic variation is comfortable across two sessions; separate limits for real events are written down.
steps.easier: Return to the familiar source or environment. Avoid formal training during an already frightening noise event.

skills.title: Noises outside and window activity
skills.goal: Notice low-level outdoor activity and recover comfortably.
skills.cue: No cue; this way if needed
skills.setup: Blinds/window film or greater distance; safe retreat into the home.

steps.title: Reduce constant exposure
steps.teach: Arrange a comfortable area farther from the window or entryway, with view screening and gentle background sound if enjoyed. Rehearse moving there for rewards when nothing is happening. Record which sounds or sights are noticed and what the dog’s comfortable baseline looks like.
steps.advance: Can use the quieter arrangement comfortably; a manageable version of the chosen outside event is identified.
steps.easier: Add more distance or view screening. This management stage need not wait for obedience training.

steps.title: Pair one manageable outside event
steps.teach: Choose a very quiet scheduled event, such as a helper’s soft footstep far outside, while your dog is in the easy area. After they notice it, promptly supply desired food. Let the event end and allow recovery. Handle unexpected loud events by reducing exposure and offering support.
steps.advance: Several brief presentations of that same low-level event stay comfortable over two sessions.
steps.easier: Make the event fainter or farther away. Do not deliberately provoke prolonged window barking to practice.

steps.title: Practice returning away from the window
steps.teach: When the low-level event is comfortable, invite a practiced turn or short move toward the resting area, then reward there. Keep also giving easy event–food pairings so hearing the sound does not mean performing a task to get relief.
steps.advance: Can comfortably notice and move away from the selected event in two easy sessions; not merely silent while tense.
steps.easier: Use more distance or return to simple pairing. Separate sight, sound, and visitor movement if the combined event is too much.

skills.title: Prepare for unavoidable noise events
skills.goal: Use a practiced refuge and support plan during storms or fireworks.
skills.setup: Discuss severe noise fear with your vet before the event; this is a management plan.

steps.title: Rehearse the support arrangement
steps.teach: On a quiet day, set up the familiar refuge, close curtains, check escape routes, and try gentle masking sound if your dog likes it. Sit nearby and let them choose to hide, rest, or seek contact. Rehearse any veterinarian-prescribed plan only as directed by that veterinarian.
steps.advance: The refuge, trusted company, and any ordinary sound masking are familiar and comfortable before the event.
steps.easier: Remove masking that worries the dog or change the resting location. A crate is suitable only if already comfortable.

steps.title: Use the plan during the real event
steps.teach: Before expected noise, bring your dog inside and use the familiar quiet setup. Stay available; offer food or play if wanted, and calm contact if sought. Do not require a posture or formal training. Afterward record observations and recovery; review poor outcomes with your vet before the next event.
steps.advance: The support plan has been used and reviewed. Marking this step complete means the plan is ready, not that noise fear is cured.
steps.easier: Increase protection and trusted support; do not test louder exposure. Panic or persistent distress calls for veterinary reassessment.

skills.title: Comfort with an object or appliance
skills.goal: Handle a gradual, voluntary introduction to one specific object.
skills.setup: Object off and stationary first; dog can leave without crossing its path.

steps.title: Start with the object still and off
steps.teach: Put the object far enough away that your dog can notice it comfortably. Reward looking or calm exploration from you, without luring closer. Let them retreat. If the object is already frightening merely at sight, use more distance or only a partial view.
steps.advance: Several brief comfortable views across two sessions; the dog can choose ordinary movement and retreat.
steps.easier: Increase distance or show less of the object. Do not place food on it to force approach.

steps.title: Add a tiny movement
steps.teach: At the comfortable distance, have a helper move the object an inch, then stop; immediately provide desired food. For a vacuum, keep it switched off here. Repeat only after baseline returns and keep the dog’s escape path clear.
steps.advance: The selected tiny movement is comfortable in multiple observations over two sessions.
steps.easier: Use a smaller movement or a more distant helper; remove motion if posture tightens.

steps.title: Introduce sound separately
steps.teach: For an appliance, begin a very faint brief recording or run it behind a distant closed door while the dog remains comfortable. Pair the noticed sound with food, then stop. Rebuild sight and sound separately before combining them at an easier level.
steps.advance: Separate sound and motion versions are comfortable; any first combination remains easy over two sessions.
steps.easier: Return to one component only or arrange for the dog to stay elsewhere during actual use.

skills.title: Bikes, moving vehicles, or joggers at a distance
skills.goal: Observe one movement trigger comfortably from a protected location.
skills.setup: Safe stationary location away from traffic; no off-leash chase practice.

steps.title: Watch a slow distant version
steps.teach: Pick one trigger type and a protected position with a clear retreat. A cooperative adult can slowly move a bicycle far away, for example. After your dog notices, promptly reward and let the view end. Do not use traffic as something to approach or chase for practice.
steps.advance: Several comfortable observations of the slow distant version in two sessions, with normal recovery.
steps.easier: Use a stationary version, more distance, or a partial view. Chasing may involve motivations beyond fear.

steps.title: Change speed or duration separately
steps.teach: Keep separation fixed and let the helper move slightly faster for a very short interval, then stop. Pair with rewards and retain easy slow versions. Change the length of the observation on a different session. Leave early if your dog starts tracking rigidly.
steps.advance: Comfortable observations of the selected speed in two sessions; physical management continues regardless of progress.
steps.easier: Return to slower motion or greater distance. Intense chase or redirection needs an individualized professional plan.

skills.title: Comfort around a parked car
skills.goal: Voluntarily enter and rest briefly in a safely parked vehicle.
skills.setup: Parked car in a comfortable temperature; doors secure; vet review for nausea/pain.

steps.title: Begin near the stationary car
steps.teach: From a comfortable distance, let your dog see the parked, switched-off vehicle and provide desired food. Gradually work toward an open door only as comfortable. Let them move away. Put non-slip footing or a suitable ramp in place if needed; never pull them inside.
steps.advance: Can approach the open car door comfortably across two sessions, without needing food held inside to lure them.
steps.easier: Work farther away, shorten the view, or seek help for existing severe travel fear.

steps.title: Teach entry and immediate exit
steps.teach: With safe footing and a reachable entrance, reward any voluntary step toward entry, then a paw inside, then full entry across small sessions. Invite an immediate easy exit and reward outside too. Do not close the door while the dog is still deciding whether to enter.
steps.advance: Voluntarily enters and exits with loose movement over several rehearsals in two sessions.
steps.easier: Use an easier entrance or ramp and smaller steps. A painful jump or forced lift is not a training solution.

steps.title: Add restraint and door movement separately
steps.teach: Introduce the familiar travel restraint while stationary and reward comfort. Separately rehearse tiny door movements, then brief closure while a trusted person stays with the dog. Engine noise and actual driving each require later gradual sessions; arrange veterinary care if nausea or panic appears.
steps.advance: Comfortable with the chosen stationary setup and brief door closure; a separate travel plan is recorded.
steps.easier: Keep the door open and reduce duration. Never leave the dog unattended or run an engine in an enclosed space.

skills.title: Comfortable harness routine
skills.goal: Voluntarily participate in putting on a well-fitted harness.
skills.setup: Comfortable fit that allows movement; clip-around style may suit head-shy dogs.

steps.title: Make equipment appearance pleasant
steps.teach: Show the harness at a comfortable distance, then give a tiny reward and put it away. Separately make the buckle click quietly at a distance and reward. Bring it nearer only while your dog remains loose and willing to approach.
steps.advance: Comfortable with the sight and buckle sound over several short rehearsals.
steps.easier: Use more distance or a quieter buckle sound. Do not bring the equipment toward a retreating dog.

steps.title: Invite voluntary fitting
steps.teach: Hold the head opening still and let your dog choose to bring the head toward or through it, rewarding small progress. For a clip-around harness, briefly touch the comfortable strap area, reward, and remove it. Build to placing the harness without fastening, then remove before worry appears.
steps.advance: Willingly participates in the selected fitting method several times with loose movement.
steps.easier: Use a larger opening or a clip-around design. Do not lure the head through and suddenly trap it.

steps.title: Fasten briefly and move
steps.teach: After comfortable placement, fasten one clip, reward, and unfasten immediately. Build to all clips and a few comfortable indoor steps, checking for rubbing or restricted movement. Remove before pawing or avoidance develops. Assess actual security and fit directly before outdoor use.
steps.advance: Comfortable fitting and a short walk in two sessions; the harness fits securely without restricting ordinary movement.
steps.easier: Shorten wear or return to unfastened placement. Equipment fit must be checked even when the dog accepts it.

skills.title: Comfortable basket muzzle
skills.goal: Wear a correctly fitted basket muzzle willingly.
skills.setup: Basket with generous pant room; drink/treat access; no unattended wear. Get help for guarding or head-handling fear.

steps.title: Make the muzzle predict food
steps.teach: Show the muzzle at a comfortable distance, give food, and remove it. Let your dog approach or leave. Reward a glance or voluntary approach without moving it onto the face. Check fit with knowledgeable help; broad head shape makes model and sizing important.
steps.advance: Approaches the visible muzzle willingly with loose posture across several rehearsals.
steps.easier: Place it farther away and reward there. Do not hold it over the face or follow the dog with it.

steps.title: Teach voluntary nose entry
steps.teach: Hold the basket still with straps out of the way. Reward a nose approach, then a shallow voluntary entry. Gradually deliver treats through the front after entry, rather than always showing food inside first. The dog can withdraw at any moment; do not fasten yet.
steps.advance: Voluntarily inserts the nose without a visible lure on 4 of 5 easy presentations in two sessions.
steps.easier: Reward shallower entries and keep the muzzle completely still. Stop for guarding or handling concerns.

steps.title: Build a few seconds and introduce straps
steps.teach: Feed through the basket while the dog chooses to keep the nose inside, starting below one second. Separately reward a quiet buckle sound and gentle strap touch. Combine a brief nose entry with a loose strap drape only when both pieces are comfortable.
steps.advance: Can choose a few seconds of nose entry and remain comfortable with strap movement in two sessions.
steps.easier: Shorten the entry or train the buckle separately. Withdrawal ends the attempt without restraint.

steps.title: Fasten and remove immediately
steps.teach: With comfortable nose entry, briefly fasten the fitted straps, feed through the basket, and unfasten at once. Repeat short successful fittings before adding one or two steps. If pawing or freezing appears, remove safely and return to an easier stage; do not wait for them to give up.
steps.advance: Comfortable brief fastening and a few steps across two sessions, with normal movement and no persistent attempts to remove it.
steps.easier: Check fit, shorten wear, or return to unfastened entry. A muzzle reduces risk but does not make a frightening situation acceptable.

steps.title: Build easy practical wear
steps.teach: During a familiar pleasant activity, increase wear by a few comfortable seconds, alternating shorter attempts. Later try a short quiet outdoor outing with ordinary distance from triggers. Continue checking full pant room, drinking, rubbing, and secure attachment throughout use.
steps.advance: Comfortable for the practical short duration you need in easy settings; fit and ongoing welfare checks are recorded.
steps.easier: Use a shorter activity or return indoors. Continue managing triggers; muzzle training does not treat their emotional cause.

skills.title: Voluntary chin rest
skills.goal: Place the chin on a hand or towel without restraint.
skills.setup: Dog comfortable with hands near the face; no painful area handling.

steps.title: Capture chin placement
steps.teach: Hold an open palm or folded towel just below chin height, without pressing upward. Reward a voluntary approach, then a light chin contact. Toss a reset reward away and offer again. If a small lure is useful, fade it early; the dog chooses contact.
steps.advance: Offers a light chin contact repeatedly without a hand moving into the face.
steps.easier: Use a towel on a low support or reward a smaller approach. Get help if face handling worries the dog.

steps.title: Add a short hold and an exit
steps.teach: Reward a half-second of voluntary chin contact, then invite a break. Build to one or two seconds with easier attempts mixed in. Add “chin” just before offering the familiar target. Lifting the chin ends the attempt; never hold it down or block withdrawal.
steps.advance: Offers and briefly holds the target on the chosen cue/signal in 4 of 5 comfortable attempts across two sessions.
steps.easier: Shorten the hold and reward sooner. This posture alone is not proof that handling feels safe.

skills.title: Cooperative gentle handling
skills.goal: Participate in a tiny, non-painful care action with a clear stop option.
skills.setup: Only healthy comfortable areas; veterinary direction for painful or urgent care.

steps.title: Make one small hand movement comfortable
steps.teach: With the dog free to leave, offer the known chin target. Move your other hand slightly toward a comfortable shoulder, then stop and reward. End hand movement immediately if the chin lifts. Wait for a voluntary new start; do not keep repositioning the dog.
steps.advance: Several small hand movements are comfortable and the handler consistently honors withdrawal.
steps.easier: Make the hand motion smaller or omit the chin signal until the dog is comfortable with the setup.

steps.title: Add a moment of gentle touch
steps.teach: After a voluntary start, touch the healthy shoulder lightly for less than a second, remove the hand, and reward. Build one feature at a time—brief duration OR a nearby body area—while continuing to stop at withdrawal. Do not use food to conceal a difficult procedure.
steps.advance: Several brief touches in two sessions are comfortable, with easy re-initiation and no avoidance after the break.
steps.easier: Use a shorter/lighter touch. Stop and consult the vet for new sensitivity or possible pain.

skills.title: Comfort with a brush or towel
skills.goal: Accept a brief gentle grooming action voluntarily.
skills.setup: Suitable gentle tool; skin healthy; dog can leave.

steps.title: Introduce the tool separately
steps.teach: Show a soft brush or towel at a comfortable distance, then reward. Put it away between presentations. After comfortable sighting, move it slightly near a healthy easy area without touching, reward, and remove. Do not begin with a tangle or a sensitive spot.
steps.advance: Comfortable with the tool’s appearance and small movement in several short sessions.
steps.easier: Use a softer tool or greater distance; ask your vet about skin discomfort.

steps.title: Try one gentle stroke
steps.teach: After a voluntary start signal or relaxed approach, give one light short stroke on a comfortable shoulder, then stop and reward. Wait for the dog to choose another turn. Gradually try two strokes, mixing single easy ones in. End at any withdrawal.
steps.advance: Repeated short grooming turns are comfortable across two sessions, with no avoidance afterward.
steps.easier: Reduce pressure or use only a momentary towel touch. Painful matting or necessary grooming needs an individualized care plan.

skills.title: Paw-care preparation
skills.goal: Be comfortable with tiny paw/tool preparations; clipping is a separate skilled procedure.
skills.setup: Non-slip surface; healthy paws; knowledgeable guidance before actual trimming.

steps.title: Start above the paw
steps.teach: With your dog free to stand or lie comfortably, briefly touch a healthy upper leg, remove the hand, and reward. Gradually work lower over separate sessions, stopping if the dog pulls away. Do not grab or hold a paw to prevent movement.
steps.advance: Light contact near the paw remains comfortable in several observations over two sessions.
steps.easier: Stay higher on the leg or use a shorter touch. New paw sensitivity needs veterinary assessment.

steps.title: Separate tool appearance from contact
steps.teach: Show the nail tool at a distance and reward; introduce its quiet sound separately if relevant. Only once comfortable, bring it slightly toward the paw, stop well short, and reward. Actual clipping or grinding is not the next automatic step: get instruction on anatomy, tool use, and this dog’s comfort.
steps.advance: Comfortable with the selected non-contact preparation in two sessions; an appropriate next-care plan is arranged.
steps.easier: Return the tool farther away or omit its sound. Never restrain the paw to finish a training repetition.

skills.title: Voluntary toothbrushing preparation
skills.goal: Build comfortable participation in gentle veterinary-guided mouth care.
skills.setup: Veterinary clearance for any dental pain; a demonstrated technique, pet-safe paste and soft suitable brush. No human toothpaste or forced jaw opening.

steps.title: Comfort with the care items
steps.teach: Let the dog see the soft brush at a comfortable distance and reward relaxed interest. Separately offer a tiny taste of veterinarian-approved pet toothpaste if suitable. Keep hands away from the mouth while building pleasant associations with the items.
steps.advance: Comfortably sees the brush and voluntarily accepts the chosen pet-safe taste if used.
steps.easier: Remove the paste, increase brush distance, or ask the veterinary team about discomfort or suitable materials.

steps.title: Invite a tiny lip touch
steps.teach: Ask your veterinary team to demonstrate a suitable safe approach. When the dog voluntarily offers their familiar chin rest or other agreed start signal, briefly touch the outer lip area as demonstrated, remove your hand, and reward. Stop immediately if the dog withdraws.
steps.advance: Freely offers repeated start signals and stays comfortable with a momentary gentle lip-area touch.
steps.easier: Return to hand movement at a distance. Pain, guarding, or resistance calls for individual help, not holding the head.

steps.title: One gentle outside-tooth stroke
steps.teach: Following the veterinary demonstration and only after comfortable lip-area work, use the soft pet brush for one gentle brief stroke on an accessible outer tooth surface. Stop, reward, and offer a break. Add tiny amounts of brushing only while participation remains voluntary.
steps.advance: Comfortably accepts one gentle demonstrated stroke and willingly returns for another invitation. Full brushing is built gradually with veterinary guidance.
steps.easier: Return to brush presence or lip-area work. Stop for pain, bleeding, tension, avoidance, or any need for restraint.

skills.title: Comfort on a floor scale
skills.goal: Choose to stand on a stable low scale surface.
skills.setup: A broad stable non-slip low veterinary or pet scale, secured against wobbling; no elevated platform or forced placement.

steps.title: Explore the low surface
steps.teach: Let the dog investigate the secured scale while it is still and quiet. Reward comfortable looking or approaching from the floor. A large flat mat beside it can make the area familiar. Do not lure an uneasy dog onto a moving or slippery surface.
steps.advance: Approaches the stable scale with loose ordinary movement and freely moves away and returns.
steps.easier: Begin with an ordinary floor mat and ask the clinic about a broader non-slip surface.

steps.title: Choose a step on and off
steps.teach: Reward a voluntary front-foot step onto the wide low surface, then invite an easy step off. Build to all four feet only if the surface stays stable and the dog moves comfortably. Never lift paws or use the leash to position the body.
steps.advance: Chooses to step on and off the broad low scale with all feet comfortably supported.
steps.easier: Reward a smaller step or return to a flat mat. Stop for wobbling, hesitation, or pain.

steps.title: A brief weigh-in pause
steps.teach: Say “scale” before the familiar approach. Reward a short comfortable stand, then release off the scale before the dog needs to shift. Add just enough time for the reading while the person stays quiet. Other clinic handling is a separate cooperative-care lesson.
steps.advance: Voluntarily steps on and briefly stands long enough for a reading in two comfortable practice sessions.
steps.easier: Release sooner, reward entry only, or work with the clinic on an easier weighing setup.

skills.title: Take a safe object
skills.goal: Pick up an offered suitable object voluntarily.
skills.setup: Light dog-safe object too large to swallow; no guarding or painful mouth.

steps.title: Shape gentle mouth contact
steps.teach: Hold the object still at an easy height. Mark a sniff initially, then reward a tiny open-mouth contact or gentle grip. Remove it between attempts. Keep criteria small enough for frequent success and never put the object into the mouth yourself.
steps.advance: Voluntarily makes a gentle grip on most easy presentations without chewing or avoidance.
steps.easier: Try a different texture or lighter object; reward smaller mouth movements. Avoid food deprivation or forced holds.

steps.title: Add take before the offer
steps.teach: Say “take,” then present the object. Mark as the dog grips and reward after a voluntary release/trade. Begin supporting less of the weight for a moment. Finish before chewing begins. This stage is pickup, not carrying it across the room.
steps.advance: Takes the object on one cue on 4 of 5 presentations across two sessions, without a visible food lure.
steps.easier: Offer at a more comfortable height and shorten the grip; practice the release separately.

skills.title: Hold gently
skills.goal: Support a light object briefly without chewing.
skills.setup: Known take and drop; use an ordinary safe toy.

steps.title: Build a supported brief hold
steps.teach: Ask for take while you lightly support the object. Mark a calm half-second grip before the dog drops it; accept the release and reward. Slowly vary between half a second and one second. Do not hold the jaw closed or pull against the dog.
steps.advance: Gently holds the supported object for about one second on most trials, without biting down or chewing.
steps.easier: Shorten the interval and use a lighter object. Reward before dropping usually occurs.

steps.title: Remove your support briefly
steps.teach: As your dog takes the object, briefly relax your hand support, then offer your receiving hand and cue drop. Reward the delivery. Build only a few seconds and add “hold” just before the familiar grip if useful. Let unsuccessful attempts reset without correction.
steps.advance: Gently supports the object unaided for about two seconds, then releases, on 4 of 5 attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Restore light support or use a shorter hold. Avoid chasing after a dropped object.

skills.title: Deliver into your hand
skills.goal: Place a held object over your open hand and release.
skills.setup: Comfortable take/drop; empty receiving palm below the object.

steps.title: Place the receiving hand under the object
steps.teach: Let your dog hold the light toy. Put an open palm just beneath it, say “give,” then use the familiar drop cue if needed. Mark the release into your hand and reward. Return the toy often so delivery does not always end the game.
steps.advance: Releases over the receiving hand with the short prompt on most easy attempts.
steps.easier: Raise the receiving palm closer without grabbing. Use a trade to preserve a comfortable release.

steps.title: Fade the extra drop cue
steps.teach: Present the palm and say “give,” then pause briefly. If your dog releases, mark and reward. If not, help with drop and make the next attempt easier. Vary hand position only a little while keeping the object close and supported if needed.
steps.advance: Delivers to your palm on the chosen cue/signal without the extra prompt on 4 of 5 attempts across two sessions.
steps.easier: Return to give followed by drop. Do not reach into the mouth or wrestle for the object.

skills.title: Carry a few steps
skills.goal: Walk a few comfortable steps holding an object, then deliver.
skills.setup: Quiet non-slip space; known gentle hold and hand delivery.

steps.title: Add one step toward you
steps.teach: Offer take, then move your receiving hand only a few inches away while you step back once. As your dog moves with the object, receive it with give and reward. Mark the completed delivery rather than interrupting the carry with an early terminal marker.
steps.advance: Carries one step and gives the item on most easy attempts.
steps.easier: Use half a step and a shorter hold. Keep your receiving hand close.

steps.title: Build a short carry
steps.teach: Alternate one-step carries with two, then three steps, rewarding each delivery. Keep the path straight and boring. If chewing starts, use a lighter item or shorten the distance. Add “bring” just before the dog starts toward you.
steps.advance: Carries a light item several steps and delivers on 4 of 5 attempts across two sessions.
steps.easier: Reduce distance and rebuild gentle holds. Avoid turning this into chase or keep-away.

skills.title: Retrieve a placed toy
skills.goal: Pick up a nearby placed toy and bring it to your hand.
skills.setup: Known carry and give; begin with a stationary item rather than a throw.

steps.title: Lower pickup toward the floor
steps.teach: Offer the known object successively lower: knee height, just above the floor, then resting on the floor while your hand is nearby. Cue take and reward a gentle pickup followed by give. Treat each lower position as a small change.
steps.advance: Picks the object up from the floor and delivers nearby on most attempts.
steps.easier: Raise it slightly or use a more grippable object. Avoid repeated failed cues.

steps.title: Add a little outward travel
steps.teach: Place the toy a few inches in front of you, cue fetch, and receive it with give. Reward delivery. Gradually place it one step farther away, alternating easy distances. A small gentle roll can be added later, without repeated sprinting or abrupt stops.
steps.advance: Retrieves a placed toy from the chosen short distance and delivers on 4 of 5 attempts across two sessions.
steps.easier: Place the toy closer or restore a hand-assisted pickup. A retrieve is optional if the dog does not enjoy carrying.

skills.title: Put toys in a basket
skills.goal: Carry one suitable toy to a low basket and release inside.
skills.setup: Low stable basket; large safe toys; no food competition.

steps.title: Drop over a nearby basket
steps.teach: Place a low basket directly under your receiving hand. Ask for a short take/give so the toy falls into the basket; mark landing inside and reward. Gradually move your receiving hand away while retaining an easy release over the basket.
steps.advance: Releases an easy held toy into the basket on most nearby attempts.
steps.easier: Use a larger lower basket or put your receiving hand back over the opening.

steps.title: Add a small carry to the basket
steps.teach: Place the toy one step from the basket. Cue the familiar pickup, guide the short carry toward the basket, then use the known release. Reward landing inside. Slowly fade your guide; add “tidy” before the predictable sequence, one toy at a time.
steps.advance: Picks up one nearby toy, carries it to the basket, and drops inside on 4 of 5 attempts across two sessions.
steps.easier: Move the toy closer or practice basket releases again. Add more toys only after one-item repetitions are enjoyable.

skills.title: Easy food search
skills.goal: Find a tiny food hide through comfortable sniffing.
skills.setup: Single dog; suitable food portion; no swallowing packaging or unsafe puzzles.

steps.title: Make the first hides obvious
steps.teach: Let your dog watch you place a few pieces of normal food on a flat towel or in open shallow containers. Say “search” and let them investigate freely. Help by revealing food if needed. Keep the first game easy enough to finish quickly.
steps.advance: Readily searches the simple layout without frustration, guarding, or trying to eat the materials.
steps.easier: Use food directly on a clean floor with no container. Keep other animals separate.

steps.title: Hide just one easy piece
steps.teach: With your dog nearby, put a piece partly behind a safe object while they watch, then cue search. Later make one similarly easy hide while they look away. Keep the search area tiny and reveal the hide if the dog stalls. End after a few rewarding finds.
steps.advance: Finds a few easy partly hidden pieces willingly and remains comfortable through the game.
steps.easier: Make the food more visible or reduce the area. This is enrichment, not a test or a cure for anxiety.

skills.title: Gentle tug with a release
skills.goal: Enjoy brief safe toy play and willingly release.
skills.setup: Suitable large toy; no pain, guarding, jumping, or suspended pulling.

steps.title: Invite a tiny low game
steps.teach: Offer a suitable toy and let your dog choose to grip. Move it gently side to side at comfortable neck height for one or two seconds, then use a familiar rewarding drop trade. Return the toy for another short turn. Skip this game if it increases tension.
steps.advance: Several brief play-and-release turns stay loose, safe, and enjoyable.
steps.easier: Use less movement or another game. A dog need not enjoy tug to learn other skills.

steps.title: Build a predictable finish
steps.teach: Alternate very short play with rewarded drops. After the final release, say “all done” and offer a quiet enjoyable activity or rest. Put the toy away without reaching into the mouth. End earlier next time if the dog has trouble disengaging.
